lead: Speech changes every few milliseconds. A plain Fourier transform over a whole recording tells us which frequencies exist but not when they occur. The short-time Fourier transform cuts speech into short overlapping frames, multiplies each frame by a window, and takes a DFT. Stacking the magnitudes of those DFTs over time gives a spectrogram: time on one axis, frequency on the other, darkness or colour for energy. This view is used in speech recognition front ends, pitch tracking, finding speech versus silence, and reading formants and harmonics by eye. Some syllabi call it the STFT.
prereq: You need 7.1 for sampling and framing and 7.2 for voiced and unvoiced sounds.

blocks.text: Speech is not stationary. The vocal tract shape changes as the tongue and lips move, so one Fourier transform over a whole sentence smears every sound into a single spectrum. The fix is to assume the signal is stationary only for a short slice. Cut the signal into frames of N samples, often 20 to 30 ms. At 16 kHz, 25 ms is 400 samples. Consecutive frames start a hop H samples apart, often 10 ms = 160 samples, so frames overlap. Overlap stops a sound falling at a frame edge from being lost.

blocks.where: w[n] is the window weight at sample n; N is the frame length in samples; n is the sample index inside the frame.

blocks.text: Before the transform, multiply the frame by a window w[n]. A rectangular window has abrupt edges and causes spectral leakage: energy from one frequency leaks into neighbouring bins. The Hamming window tapers the edges. Its value is about 0.08 at the frame edges and 1.0 at the centre. The windowed frame is x<sub>w</sub>[n] = x[n]·w[n].

items: Choose sampling rate fs, frame length in samples N, and hop H in samples.
Take frame m as x[n] for n = mH to mH + N − 1.
Multiply the frame by the Hamming window to get x<sub>w</sub>[n].
Take the DFT of x<sub>w</sub>[n] and keep the magnitude for this time position.

sections.h3: One DFT per frame and the spectrogram

blocks.where: X<sub>m</sub>[k] is the DFT of frame m at bin k; x<sub>w</sub>[n] is the windowed frame; N is the DFT length; k is the bin index from 0 to N−1; j is √−1.

blocks.text: Bin k represents a frequency near k·fs/N. The bin spacing is fs/N hertz. With fs = 16 kHz and N = 512, one bin is 31.25 Hz wide. For a real signal, bins k = 0 to N/2 are non-redundant; the rest are mirror images. Zero-padding a 400-sample frame to 512 points gives a finer display grid but does not improve true frequency resolution. True resolution is set by the window length, not by the DFT length.

A spectrogram is made by placing the magnitude |X<sub>m</sub>[k]| of each frame as one vertical column and moving to the next frame in time. This is the short-time Fourier transform. The frame length controls a trade-off. A wide-band spectrogram uses a short window, about 5 ms. It has good time resolution and poor frequency resolution, so it shows pitch pulses and formants as broad bands. A narrow-band spectrogram uses a long window, about 45 ms. It has good frequency resolution and poor time resolution, so it shows individual harmonics as horizontal lines.

sections.h3: Short-time energy, zero-crossing rate, pitch and boundaries

blocks.text: Two cheap frame-level measures separate speech from silence and voiced from unvoiced. Short-time energy is E = (1/N) Σ x²[n]. It is large in vowels and weak in silence. Zero-crossing rate is ZCR = (1/(N−1)) Σ |sgn(x[n]) − sgn(x[n−1])|/2. It is high for unvoiced sounds such as /s/ and low for voiced sounds and silence.
R(τ) = Σ<sub>n</sub> x[n]·x[n+τ],   τ* = argmax R(τ),   F0 = fs/τ*
blocks.where: R(τ) is the autocorrelation at lag τ samples; τ* is the lag with the largest autocorrelation in the allowed pitch range; F0 is the fundamental frequency in hertz; fs is the sampling rate in hertz.

blocks.text: For a voiced frame, the waveform repeats after one pitch period. Autocorrelation measures that repetition. Search τ over the plausible pitch range, take the lag with the largest R(τ), and convert it to F0. Energy dips between words give candidate word boundaries, but a real boundary needs the lexicon and language model of 7.6. Energy alone also drops inside weak sounds, so it over-segments.

figure.caption: One 25 ms frame of 400 samples is windowed, transformed by a 512-point DFT, and turned into one column of a spectrogram. The spectrogram is the stack of such columns over time.

spec.title: From one frame to one spectrogram column
spec.aria: One frame of speech is windowed, transformed by a DFT, and its magnitude becomes one column of a spectrogram.

examples.question: Speech is sampled at fs = 16000 Hz. A frame is 25 ms long and the hop is 10 ms. The DFT length is 512. For 1.00 s of speech: (a) find the frame length and hop in samples, (b) find the bin spacing, (c) find the number of frames, (d) find the number of non-redundant DFT bins and the number of positive-frequency bins after dropping DC, (e) list the first three harmonic frequencies for a voiced frame with F0 = 125 Hz and the DFT bin nearest to each.
steps: Frame length in samples = fs × 25 ms = 16000 × 0.025 = 400 samples.
Hop in samples = fs × 10 ms = 16000 × 0.010 = 160 samples.
Bin spacing = fs/N = 16000/512 = 31.25 Hz per bin.
Number of frames = floor((16000 − 400)/160) + 1 = floor(15600/160) + 1 = floor(97.5) + 1 = 97 + 1 = 98 frames.
Non-redundant bins for a real signal = N/2 + 1 = 512/2 + 1 = 257 bins, k = 0 to 256.
Positive-frequency bins after dropping DC = 257 − 1 = 256 bins.
examples.answer: The frame is 400 samples, the hop is 160 samples, the bin spacing is 31.25 Hz, there are 98 frames, 257 non-redundant bins (256 after dropping DC), and harmonics at 125 Hz, 250 Hz and 375 Hz, nearest bins 4, 8 and 12.
examples.check:
import math
fs = 16000
win_ms = 25
hop_ms = 10
N = 512
dur = 1.0
F0 = 125
win = int(round(fs * win_ms / 1000))
hop = int(round(fs * hop_ms / 1000))
binsp = fs / N
frames = math.floor((fs * dur - win) / hop) + 1
nonred = N // 2 + 1
pos = nonred - 1
h1 = F0
h2 = 2 * F0
h3 = 3 * F0
print(win)
print(hop)
print(binsp)
print(frames)
print(nonred)
print(pos)
print(h1)
print(h2)
print(h3)
print(int(round(h1 / binsp)))
print(int(round(h2 / binsp)))
print(int(round(h3 / binsp)))

traps: Confusing window length with hop length: a 25 ms window and 10 ms hop give overlapping frames, not separate blocks.
Believing zero-padding improves frequency resolution. Going from 400 to 512 points only interpolates the spectrum; resolution is set by the 25 ms window.
Reversing the spectrogram trade-off: wide-band uses a short window, has good time resolution and poor frequency resolution; narrow-band uses a long window and shows harmonics.
Forgetting that a real DFT of length N has N/2 + 1 non-redundant bins, not N/2, when DC and Nyquist are included.
Treating every energy dip as a word boundary. Weak sounds also have low energy; the lexicon and language model decide real word boundaries.

quiz.a: A time-frequency picture made by stacking the magnitude spectra of short, windowed frames; time is one axis and frequency is the other.

quiz.q: Why multiply a frame by a Hamming window before the DFT?
quiz.a: The taper reduces abrupt frame edges, which reduces spectral leakage into neighbouring bins. It makes the spectrum cleaner.

quiz.q: Speech is sampled at 8 kHz. The frame is 20 ms, the hop is 10 ms, and the DFT length is 256. Find the frame length in samples, hop in samples, and bin spacing.
quiz.a: Frame = 8000 × 0.020 = 160 samples. Hop = 8000 × 0.010 = 80 samples. Bin spacing = 8000/256 = 31.25 Hz.

quiz.q: A spectrogram shows pitch pulses clearly but harmonics are blurred. Which window length is likely, and why?
quiz.a: A short window, about 5 ms, was used. Short windows give good time resolution, so pitch pulses show, but poor frequency resolution, so harmonics blur together.

quiz.q: What does the lag at the maximum of the autocorrelation function give for a voiced frame?
quiz.a: It gives the pitch period in samples. F0 is fs divided by that lag.

quiz.q: A voiced frame has F0 = 200 Hz and fs = 16000 Hz. What is the pitch period in samples?
Why is a single energy dip not enough to declare a word boundary?
quiz.a: Weak speech sounds and silence inside words also lower energy, so energy alone over-segments. A real boundary needs lexical and language-model evidence, as in 7.6.

beyond: Not for the exam. In practice, speech tools compute the STFT with fast FFT libraries and often store only magnitudes. Modern neural systems may learn features directly from waveforms, but spectrograms remain a common input and a debugging view. Search for short-time Fourier transform, spectrogram, pitch tracking and voice activity detection to go further. The next step in this unit is to warp the frequency axis to match hearing.
